title: Phish Residency at Sphere — 2026
tagline: Nine nights. Zero repeats. A fan experience as unpredictable as the band.

body: Phish fans follow the band from city to city because no two shows are ever the same — that unpredictability is the brand. Two years after our first run, Phish returned to Sphere for nine shows over three weekends with not one song repeated: 161 unique songs, more than 27 hours of music, and a fanbase that would notice anything that felt recycled.

Any jam could stretch from four minutes to thirty, so the visuals couldn't be playback — they had to follow the band in the moment, the way the fans do. And our 2024 run had already set the bar: every song needed its own world, on the largest high-resolution screen on the planet, every single night.

The idea was to make the venue feel like part of the band. I led the project end to end as creative and delivery lead, directing a global team of 50+ artists across multiple studios and steering 70+ visual pieces from concept through nine nights of show direction — with one rule: everything had to feel like Phish, never like a tech demo.

The centerpiece was a virtual light rig: a real-time engine that recreated a physical light show across Sphere's 160,000 sq ft screen, with 7,000+ virtual lights played live by the band's longtime lighting designer, so the visuals improvised alongside the music. Around it we built worlds drawn from the band's own lore — iridescent spiderwebs, bubblegum universes, a hot-dog spaceship odyssey — anchored by high-resolution capture of The Barn, Phish's Vermont studio. Every night became something fans could only have caught in that room.
led: 01 — Creative and delivery lead, accountable for the fan experience every night
02 — Directed 50+ artists across multiple studios and 70+ visual pieces
03 — Created the real-time virtual light rig that let the visuals improvise with the band
04 — Led show direction across nine sold-out nights

impact.note: GQ said we "reinvented Sphere forever." Nine sold-out nights, 150,000+ fans in the room and 161 songs without a single repeat — proof that a show can deepen a fanbase's bond with a band, not just entertain it.
